analysis.one_liner: Closes tax breaks that let oil and gas companies lower their U.S. taxes on foreign drilling profits.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the Senate in August 2026 and referred to the Finance Committee, where it sits with no cosponsors and no action taken.
analysis.plain_summary: Multinational oil and gas companies can currently lower their U.S. tax bill using special rules for income earned from drilling abroad. This bill would close several of those openings: it would count foreign oil and gas extraction income that U.S. companies earn through foreign subsidiaries for tax purposes, extend the rules to cover tar sands and oil shale, and limit the ability of companies to count payments to foreign governments (payments made in exchange for drilling rights) as tax payments that reduce their U.S. taxes. The money these companies would otherwise shelter would instead become taxable in the United States.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers benefit in the sense that the bill raises revenue by closing tax breaks used by large oil and gas companies, meaning the tax burden these companies bear would rise and fewer profits would be sheltered. Communities affected by fossil fuel extraction would also see no new favors for tar sands and oil shale production.

how_it_helps.text: It removes the special exclusion of foreign oil and gas extraction income from the tax base of foreign corporations that U.S. shareholders own, so those profits are counted when computing tax due on global intangible low-taxed income.

It applies the dual-capacity rules so that payments oil companies make to foreign governments in exchange for drilling rights can only be credited as taxes up to what a normal taxpayer in that country would pay, limiting the use of foreign levies to reduce U.S. tax.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational oil and gas companies would pay more U.S. tax on their foreign extraction income, including income from tar sands and oil shale, and could no longer count payments to foreign governments for drilling rights as tax payments to reduce their U.S. bill. Some portion of higher costs could eventually be passed to consumers, though the bill itself does not change prices.

drawbacks.text: The tighter dual-capacity rules (Section 4) replace an existing subsection and apply prospectively; companies with existing foreign operations face compliance changes and potentially higher effective tax rates, which the industry argues can discourage foreign investment by U.S.-based energy firms.
The bill has no cosponsors and sits in the Senate Finance Committee with no scheduled action, so even supporters would acknowledge it is very unlikely to advance in this Congress.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — closing tax breaks that let oil and gas companies reduce their U.S. taxes on foreign extraction profits — is real but modest, and the revenue it raises would be borne by a concentrated industry. The main drawbacks are contested business effects: it could raise operating costs for U.S.-headquartered multinationals competing abroad, and this Congress is unlikely to even vote on it. No public service cuts or consumer price effects are specified in the bill text, but opponents would argue costs could be passed on at the pump over time.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and not a single cosponsor.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 6, 2026, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee; the action history shows no further steps.
No senators have signed on as cosponsors.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies that use these foreign tax credit rules keep paying lower U.S. taxes on foreign extraction income; no one else gains from the bill sitting still.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies using these tax rules

for.name: Sen. Martin Heinrich
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and its provisions closing the foreign oil and gas tax rules.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action on it — no hearing, markup, or floor consideration has been scheduled.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.what_they_did: The industry historically opposes efforts to tighten foreign tax credit and dual-capacity rules, which reduce the tax cost of its overseas operations.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no cosponsors of either party, so the record shows no partisan or coalition pattern yet — only a single Democratic sponsor.

industries.note: The bill narrows the foreign tax credit carve-outs and dual-capacity tax rules these companies use to lower their U.S. tax bill on foreign extraction profits, including tar sands and oil shale. It raises their effective tax cost with no offsetting benefit.

industries.industry: Oil shale and tar sands extraction
industries.note: The bill explicitly extends the tighter tax definitions to cover minerals from oil shale and tar sands, closing a definitional gap those producers could otherwise use.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since its August 2026 introduction, the bill is very unlikely to receive a hearing or vote before the 119th Congress ends in January 2027. Most tax bills at this stage die quietly in committee unless attached to a larger tax or spending package.
